{{Short description|Statistical measure of variability}}
{{for|other statistical measures also abbreviated as "MAD"|Average absolute deviation}}

In [[statistics]], the '''median absolute deviation''' ('''MAD'''), also referred to as the '''median absolute deviation from the median''' ('''MADFM'''), is a [[Robust statistics|robust]] or [[outlier (statistics)|outlier]]-resistant measure of the [[statistical dispersion|variability]] of a [[univariate]] sample of [[quantitative data]]. 
For a univariate data set ''X''<sub>1</sub>,&nbsp;''X''<sub>2</sub>,&nbsp;...,&nbsp;''X<sub>n</sub>'', the MAD is defined as the [[median]] of the [[absolute deviation]]s from the data's median, <math>\operatorname{MAD} = \operatorname{median}( |X_i - \tilde{X}|)</math>.
It can also refer to the [[statistical population|population]] [[parameter]] that is [[statistical estimation|estimated]] by the MAD calculated from a sample.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Dodge |first1=Yadolah |title=The concise encyclopedia of statistics |date=2010 |publisher=Springer |location=New York |isbn=978-0-387-32833-1 }}</ref>

==Example==

Consider the data (1, 1, 2, '''2''', 4, 6, 9). It has a median value of 2. The absolute deviations about 2 are (1, 1, 0, 0, 2, 4, 7) which in turn have a median value of 1 (because the sorted absolute deviations are (0, 0, 1, '''1''', 2, 4, 7)). So the median absolute deviation for this data is 1.

==Uses==
The median absolute deviation is a measure of [[statistical dispersion]]. Moreover, the MAD is a [[robust statistic]], being more resilient to outliers in a data set than the [[standard deviation]]. In the standard deviation, the distances from the [[mean]] are squared, so large deviations are weighted more heavily, and thus outliers can heavily influence it. In the MAD, the deviations of a small number of outliers are irrelevant.

Because the MAD is a more robust estimator of scale than the sample [[variance]] or [[standard deviation]], it works better with distributions without a mean or variance, such as the [[Cauchy distribution]].

== Relation to standard deviation ==

The MAD may be used similarly to how one would use the deviation for the average.
In order to use the MAD as a [[consistent estimator]] for the [[Scale parameter#Estimation|estimation]] of the [[standard deviation]] <math>\sigma</math>, one takes

: <math>\hat{\sigma} = k \cdot \operatorname{MAD},</math>

where <math>k</math> is a constant [[scale factor]], which depends on the distribution.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Rousseeuw | first1 = P. J. |author-link=Peter Rousseeuw | last2 = Croux | first2 = C. | year = 1993 | title = Alternatives to the median absolute deviation | journal = Journal of the American Statistical Association | volume = 88 | issue = 424| pages = 1273–1283 | doi = 10.1080/01621459.1993.10476408 | hdl = 2027.42/142454 | hdl-access = free }}</ref>

For [[normal distribution|normally distributed]] data <math>k</math> is taken to be
: <math>k = 1/\left(\Phi^{-1}(3/4)\right) \approx 1/0.67449 \approx 1.4826,</math>
i.e., the [[multiplicative inverse|reciprocal]] of the [[quantile function]] <math>\Phi^{-1}</math> (also known as the inverse of the [[cumulative distribution function]]) for the [[standard normal distribution]] <math>Z = (X - \mu) / \sigma</math>.<ref name="google">{{cite book |title=Statistics and Data Analysis for Financial Engineering |author=Ruppert, D. |date=2010 |publisher=Springer |isbn=9781441977878 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=i2bD50PbIikC&pg=PA118 |page=118 |access-date=2015-08-27}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Leys | first1 = C. | display-authors = etal   | year = 2013 | title = Detecting outliers: Do not use standard deviation around the mean, use absolute deviation around the median | url = https://dipot.ulb.ac.be/dspace/bitstream/2013/139499/1/Leys_MAD_final-libre.pdf| journal = Journal of Experimental Social Psychology | volume = 49| issue = 4| pages = 764–766| doi = 10.1016/j.jesp.2013.03.013 }}</ref>

===Derivation===
The argument 3/4 is such that <math>\pm \operatorname{MAD}</math> covers 50% (between 0.25 and 0.75) of the standard normal [[cumulative distribution function]], i.e.
: <math>\frac 12 = P(|X - \mu| \le \operatorname{MAD}) = P\left(\left|\frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}\right| \le \frac {\operatorname{MAD}} \sigma\right) = P\left(|Z| \le \frac{\operatorname{MAD}}{\sigma}\right).</math>
Therefore, we must have that
: <math>\Phi\left(\operatorname{MAD} / \sigma\right) - \Phi\left(-\operatorname{MAD} / \sigma\right) = 1/2.</math>
Noticing that
: <math>\Phi\left(-\operatorname{MAD} / \sigma\right) = 1 - \Phi\left(\operatorname{MAD} / \sigma\right),</math>
we have that <math>\operatorname{MAD} / \sigma = \Phi^{-1}(3/4) = 0.67449</math>, from which we obtain the scale factor <math>k = 1 / \Phi^{-1}(3/4) = 1.4826</math>.

Another way of establishing the relationship is noting that MAD equals the [[half-normal distribution]] median:
: <math>\operatorname{MAD} = \sigma\sqrt{2}\operatorname{erf}^{-1}(1/2) \approx 0.67449 \sigma.</math>
This form is used in, e.g., the [[probable error]].

In the case of [[Complex number|complex]] values (''X''+i''Y''), the relation of MAD to the standard deviation is unchanged for normally distributed data.

== Multivariate generalization ==
Analogously to how the [[median]] generalizes to the [[geometric median]] (GM) in [[multivariate data]], MAD can be generalized to the ''median of distances to GM'' (MADGM) in ''n'' dimensions. This is done by replacing the absolute differences in one dimension by [[Euclidean distance]]s between the data points and the geometric median in ''n'' dimensions.<ref name="Spacek">{{cite web |last1=Spacek |first1=Libor |title=Rstats - Rust Implementation of Statistical Measures, Vector Algebra, Geometric Median, Data Analysis and Machine Learning |url=https://crates.io/crates/rstats |website=crates.io |access-date=26 July 2022 |ref=6}}</ref> This gives the identical result as the univariate MAD in one dimension and generalizes to any number of dimensions. MADGM needs the geometric median to be found, which is done by an iterative process.

== The population MAD ==

The population MAD is defined analogously to the sample MAD, but is based on the complete population rather than on a sample. For a symmetric distribution with zero mean, the population MAD is the 75th [[percentile]] of the distribution.

Unlike the [[population variance|variance]], which may be infinite or undefined, the population MAD is always a finite number. For example, the standard [[Cauchy distribution]] has undefined variance, but its MAD is 1.

The earliest known mention of the concept of the MAD occurred in 1816, in a paper by [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] on the determination of the accuracy of numerical observations.<ref>{{cite journal
  | last = Gauss  | first = Carl Friedrich  | author-link = Carl Friedrich Gauss
  | title = Bestimmung der Genauigkeit der Beobachtungen
  | journal = Zeitschrift für Astronomie und Verwandte Wissenschaften
  | volume = 1  | pages = 187–197
  | date = 1816 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book
  | last = Walker | first = Helen 
  | title = Studies in the History of the Statistical Method
  | publisher = Williams & Wilkins Co | date = 1931 | location = Baltimore, MD
  | pages = 24–25 }}</ref>
